paragraphs: Scope and boundaries: This page covers only O*NET-SOC 39-4031.00, Morticians, Undertakers, and Funeral Arrangers, who arrange and direct individual funeral services. It excludes embalmers specializing in embalming and restorative work, funeral attendants primarily providing on-site guidance and handling assistance, and funeral home managers responsible for business operations and compliance. Handling and embalming remains, filing legal documents, and arranging religious rites must follow licensing requirements, organizational procedures, and local laws.

How to assess fit: Using an entirely fictional list of service needs and charges, see whether you can prepare an interview outline, service plan and fee explanation, document checklist, ceremony arrangements, and handover steps, and identify three confirmation points and ways to handle changes. Keep this a paper exercise without using real information about deceased people or their families, or real legal documents.

Who may fit: People who maintain respect and organization amid grief and pressure, willingly confirm and record each family preference, engage with regulatory and form details, and coordinate families, cemeteries, clergy, and colleagues to move arrangements forward. Note: If maintaining stability in emotionally intense situations or handling regulatory and document details is difficult, compare adjacent fields first.

Note: All exercises below are editorially designed paper simulations. They involve no real remains, families, or institutional documents and do not authorize handling remains, embalming, legal filings, or religious rites. Decisions involving law, sanitation, religion, or qualifications must follow the competent authorities, organizational procedures, and local rules.

The official definition of Morticians, Undertakers, and Funeral Arrangers (O*NET-SOC 39-4031.00) is to arrange and direct individual funeral services, including coordinating transportation of remains to a mortuary, interviewing families or other authorized people to confirm details, selecting pallbearers, helping identify the officiant for religious rites, and providing transportation for mourners. The scope excludes embalmers specializing in embalming and restorative work, funeral attendants primarily providing on-site guidance and handling assistance, and funeral home managers responsible for business operations and compliance.

entries: Family communication and needs confirmation: Interview families or other authorized people to confirm details such as obituary wording, casket selection, and service plans, and provide information about funeral service options, products, and merchandise.

Transport and care of remains: Remove remains from the place of death, supervise their preparation and care, and perform embalming when necessary; direct preparation and transportation of remains for burial out of state.
Legal documents and permits: Obtain and verify the information required for legal documents such as death certificates or burial permits, complete required filings, and retain records.

Ceremonies and on-site arrangements: Plan and coordinate funerals, burials, or cremations; arrange clergy, pallbearers, and transportation for mourners; plan casket placement, lighting, and floral arrangements; and welcome or seat guests during services.

Cemetery and transportation coordination: Contact cemeteries to arrange grave opening and closing times, and arrange transportation between locations for remains, mourners, pallbearers, clergy, and floral arrangements.

Fees, accounts, and counseling: Maintain financial records, order merchandise, and prepare accounts; provide counsel and comfort to bereaved families or friends and inform survivors about benefits they may be entitled to.
Operations and staff management: Manage funeral home operations, including hiring, training, or supervising embalmers, funeral attendants, and other staff, and participate in community activities.

paragraphs: Work context (O*NET survey): 77% of respondents report constant contact with others at work; 74% consider the impact of their work on coworkers or employers very important; 65% report substantial freedom to make decisions without supervision; 74% consider teamwork extremely important; 42% encounter contaminants daily; 23% rate the consequences of error as extremely serious and 31% as very serious; 81% report that their work is not automated at all, and 13% work in enclosed vehicles daily.

Key capabilities: Listen and clearly explain service plans and fees amid grief and pressure; process documents and filings item by item in accordance with regulations; coordinate families, cemeteries, clergy, and suppliers; support the care of remains and sanitation requirements according to standards; and maintain traceable communication and service records. Knowledge of funeral service regulations, ceremonial practices, and service operations is required.

Preparation and training: O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone 3, typically requiring vocational school training, related work experience, or an associate degree, plus 1—2 years of on-the-job training (SVP 6.0 to <7.0). The O*NET national training directory lists funeral service and mortuary science programs at multiple institutions, ranging from certificates to bachelor's degrees. Most US states have additional licensing and examination requirements for morticians or funeral directors.

Professional judgment: Key decisions concern family wishes and authorization, clear explanations of services and fees, accurate legal document information, compliant care of remains and sanitation procedures, and fulfillment of religious and ceremonial requirements. Confirm before acting when uncertain or beyond your authority; escalate to a supervisor or refer to licensed personnel when needed.

Main outputs: Funeral services delivered according to family-confirmed plans; timely filings such as death certificates and burial permits; records of transportation and care of remains; ceremony and transportation arrangements; and traceable fee, accounting, and operational documents.

Conclusion: The core output of morticians, undertakers, and funeral arrangers is arranging and delivering funeral services according to family-confirmed plans, with responsibility for document filings and fee explanations. Embalmers focus on embalming and restorative work; funeral attendants primarily provide on-site guidance and assistance; funeral home managers handle operations and compliance; clergy focus on religious rites and spiritual support; meeting, convention, and event planners serve commercial events; and medical and health services managers run healthcare facilities. Adjacent occupations are presented for comparison only and do not imply automatic transfers or mutual recognition of qualifications.
The comparison draws on the official O*NET 39-4031.00 description and tasks and the O*NET profiles of adjacent occupations. It is an editorial synthesis, not a job recommendation.
Comparison dimensions: This page compares core work and outputs, key differences from this occupation, and which preferences each option may better suit, to help clarify your direction.

Difference from Embalmers: This occupation covers family communication, service arrangements, document filings, and ceremony coordination, with care of remains as one component. Embalmers specialize in embalming, disinfection, and restorative work and are generally subject to separate licensing and sanitation standards.

If you prefer specializing in embalming and restorative work, compare embalmers; if you prefer on-site guidance and assistance, compare funeral attendants; if you prefer business operations and compliance management, compare funeral home managers; if you prefer religious and spiritual support, compare clergy.

components.work_context_block: Work context (O*NET survey): 77% of respondents report constant contact with others at work; 74% consider the impact of their work on coworkers or employers very important; 65% report substantial freedom to make decisions without supervision; 74% consider teamwork extremely important; 33% consider coordinating or leading others extremely important and 47% very important; 42% encounter contaminants daily; 23% rate the consequences of error as extremely serious and 31% as very serious; 64% spend about half their working time standing; and 81% report that their work is not automated at all.

badges: Care of remains and legal documents

description.text: Morticians, undertakers, and funeral arrangers (O*NET 39-4031.00) arrange and direct individual funeral services, confirm details with families, obtain information for legal documents, and coordinate transportation, embalming, and care of remains. This page explains official tasks and work context, the US BLS 2025 median annual wage of US$55,010 and 3% growth for 2024—2034, mainland Chinese proxy wages for resident services, repairs, and other services, AI task boundaries, fit signals, and entry routes.

subject.name: Morticians, Undertakers, and Funeral Arrangers
subject.summary: Morticians, undertakers, and funeral arrangers (O*NET-SOC 39-4031.00) arrange and direct individual funeral services: interview families or other authorized people to confirm details; obtain information for legal documents such as death certificates and burial permits; coordinate transportation, embalming, and care of remains; contact cemeteries and clergy officiating ceremonies; arrange pallbearers and transportation for mourners; and maintain financial records and daily funeral home operations.
